title: Syria court sentences Assad-era grand mufti to life in prison
description: A court in Syria has sentenced the country's former top Muslim cleric to life in prison after convicting him of crimes including inciting civil war an
body: A court in Syria has sentenced the country's former top Muslim cleric to life in prison after convicting him of crimes including inciting civil war and complicity in intentional killing.Ahmed Hassoun, 77, was grand mufti between 2005 and 2021, during the rule of ousted president Bashar al-Assad.The Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus found the official religious establishment that he led was used to "provide cover" for regime military and security operations during the 13-year war, including the dropping of barrel bombs, state news agency Sana reported.Hassoun, who denied the charges, is the 10th Assad-era figure to be sentenced under Syria's transitional authorities.Assad himself, who fled to Russia after being overthrown by rebel forces two years ago, was sentenced to death in absentia for war crimes and crimes against humanity earlier this month.Judge Fakhr al-Din al-Aryan told the court that Hassoun's case was examined against the background of events that began when the regime crushed a peaceful pro-democracy uprising against Assad in 2011 with lethal force, sparking a devastating civil war in which more than 600,000 people were killed and 12 million others were forced to flee their homes."The court found that the official religious establishment, headed by the office of the mufti, had been used to provide religious cover for military and security operations and justify them publicly, including the use of barrel bombs against populated areas," Sana reported. Barrel bombs are large cylindrical containers filled with explosives. According to one monitoring group, almost 82,000 barrel bombs were dropped by regime aircraft on rebel-held areas between 2012 and 2021, killing more than 11,000 civilians.Prosecutors accused Hassoun of inciting violence against civilians and supporting the regime at religious lectures and public meetings, and in statements and media interviews.They cited an interview with Syrian TV during the battle of Aleppo in 2015, when he told civilians to leave the rebel-held east of the city and said that "every area from which a shell is fired should be completely destroyed".The court also found that the former grand mufti had "received money and gifts in exchange for intervening to secure the release of civilians detained by security agencies", and regularly provided financial support to a pro-regime militia, Liwa al-Quds, according to Sana.Hassoun told the court that video clips had been taken out of context and that he had tried to save people from the regime.Judge Aryan sentenced Hassoun to life in prison for inciting civil war and sectarian strife. He was also sentenced to 20 years for incitement to intentional killing, 10 years for principal participation in intentional killing, and three years for abuse of office.On 11 August, Assad, his brother Maher and seven other former senior figures in his regime were convicted of crimes against humanity and sentenced to death by the same court. However, the only defendant tried in person was Atef Najib, a cousin of Assad and the former head of the Political Security intelligence agency in the southern city of Deraa.Wassim Assad, another cousin and commander of a pro-regime militia, was sentenced to death in person the following week after being convicted of crimes including murder.The trials have given Syrians some sense of justice in a country where many were frustrated with the lack of accountability for the crimes committed during the civil war. But human rights activists have called for more transparency on how the verdicts were reached.In a separate development on Monday, the United States said it had rescinded its designation of Syria as a State Sponsor of Terrorism after 47 years, in line with President Donald Trump's promise to deliver sanctions relief.Interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa's Islamist group, Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), was also removed from the list of Specially Designated Global Terrorist organisations.HTS, formerly known as al-Nusra Front, was al-Qaeda's affiliate in Syria until Sharaa severed ties with the jihadist network in 2016. In late 2024, HTS led the rebel offensive that overthrew Assad and it dominates Sharaa's transitional administration."Today's action will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.Last year, the US revoked the designation of HTS as a Foreign Terrorist Organisation and removed Sharaa from its list of Specially Designated Global Terrorists.

schema.headline: Syria court sentences Assad-era grand mufti to life in prison

title: Chan Mathok Atak pleads guilty over Channel boat with 165 migrants
description: Prosecutors said Atak created a risk of death or serious personal injury to others on board the boat. Endangerment at sea is a new offence created to
body: Prosecutors said Atak created a risk of death or serious personal injury to others on board the boat. Endangerment at sea is a new offence created to target those alleged to have steered small boats over the Channel.At the time of the crossing, the dinghy set a record for the largest number of people brought over in a single boat since dinghy arrivals began on the south coast in recent years.The figure has since been surpassed, and earlier this month, a record 230 people reached the UK in a so-called "mega dinghy".Atak is due to be sentenced on 11 September.Follow BBC Kent on Facebook, external,  X, external, and on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Kent on Sounds. title: UK missiles offer may help Ukraine - but they are not what Zelensky needs most
description: The weapons are not new – they were developed in the 1990's - and they are expensive – at around £1m a piece.They also rely on complex global supply c
body: The weapons are not new – they were developed in the 1990's - and they are expensive – at around £1m a piece.They also rely on complex global supply chains and have been built in peacetime at relatively low rates – in the hundreds, not the thousands.Even with the blueprints, Ukraine may find it hard to source components. It could take months, possibly years to make the cruise missile themselves.Copying Western weapons production in peacetime is, in fact, no way to win a war. Even Nato nations now realise that.Britain and many of its allies have tended to produce small quantities of highly advanced, expensive missiles which would quickly run out in any protracted conflict.In 2021, the former head of the US Army in Europe, Gen Ben Hodges, said that in a Nato wargame the UK military ran out of key weapons within a matter of days.Proof of the recent change in mindset is the UK military is no longer buying Storm Shadow missiles for itself.Instead, under Project Brakestop, it is developing its own long-range cruise missiles, free of foreign components, and less than half the price of a Storm Shadow.Project Brakestop is also being done at break-neck speed. The UK hopes to have a new cruise missile ready by the end of the year. It is promising to supply the new weapon to Ukraine.It is Ukraine which has shown the world how to produce relatively cheap, mass produced weapons, necessary for a long, protracted conflict.Douglas Barrie, Senior Fellow for Military Aerospace at the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) told the BBC: "The decision to share UK classified information on the MBDA SCALP missiles with Ukraine, as France and Ukraine work toward local assembly lines in Ukraine, is notable. Any impact, however, will in part depend on how quickly Ukrainian assembled SCALP cruise missiles can be introduced into service."Given that Ukraine has already operated both Storm Shadow and SCALP, familiarity with the missile may help speed the overall process, but this will also be dependent on the extent and pace at which local assembly can be established."At the start of the war its armed forces relied on old Cold War-era Soviet weaponry.A slow supply of Western weapons helped it adapt. But now Ukraine produces 70% of its own weapons.Key has been its rapid development of drone technology – from small First Person View (FPV) one-way attack drones for the front line, to larger long-range drones capable of striking deep into Russian territory, further than Storm Shadows can strike.Kyiv is on track to build 10 million drones by the end of this year. And they can do it cheaper than the West, by using mass-produced Chinese parts.Nato allies' equivalent drones can be twice as expensive as they try to shun Chinese components.However, there are still weapons that Ukraine needs and struggles to produce on its own. From fast fighter jets to the most urgent example, interceptors to take down Russian ballistic missilesThe most effective weapon to do that, by far, is the US-made Patriot interceptor. Ukraine has all but run out of them and Russian ballistic missiles now make it through Ukrainian air defences with ease.America's war in Iran has meant they're in even shorter supply.They're also expensive – at around £3m a missile – and production rates have been slow. The US is planning to double production rates from around 600 Patriot missiles per annum to 2,000, but that will take several years.President Donald Trump signalled last month that he would be willing to share Patriot technology with Ukraine, but has since rowed back.Even if he had given approval, it would have taken a while for Ukraine to make Patriots themselves -  some estimate at least a year. Ukraine would also be relying on the same sophisticated  components that are in high demand across the globe.Ukraine has embarked on a programme to develop its own interceptor missiles with European support – known as Project Freya.But there are huge technological challenges in building a high-speed missile to take down another missile travelling at thousands of miles per hour. It is expensive and often time consuming.Ukraine's military and its weapons manufacturers have shown themselves to be fast learners.One of its own companies, Fire Point, is developing its own ballistic missiles which it hopes will be ready to fire in anger next year.But Russia has already ramped up its own ballistic missile production, to around 100 a month.Developing sophisticated weapons is expensive and cannot be done quickly. Ukraine is short of both time and money.So, the move to hand missile blueprints to Ukraine will be welcome, but it is not an immediate fix for Ukraine's most pressing problems, and it wwill not dramatically alter Kyiv's ability to strike Russia in new ways.

schema.headline: UK missiles offer may help Ukraine - but they are not what Zelensky needs most

title: Hawk fire: 90,000 told to evacuate as wildfire approaches Reno, Nevada
description: Figure caption, Plumes of smoke seen over Reno as thousands evacuate due to wildfiresByBen HattonUpdated 2 hours agoTens of thousands of people have b
body: Figure caption, Plumes of smoke seen over Reno as thousands evacuate due to wildfiresByBen HattonUpdated 2 hours agoTens of thousands of people have been told to evacuate from an area close to Reno, Nevada, as a large wildfire reached the outskirts of the city. Around 42,000 people have been ordered to leave their homes immediately, with a further 45,000 people urged to get ready to leave.Officials warned the fire was expected to burn for two more days and said there was no timeline for people to return to their homes.The fire, which was first reported on Saturday morning, had so far injured six people, officials said. Windy and unpredictable weather conditions have contributed to its spread.Nevada's Governor Joe Lombardo has declared a state of emergency in Washoe County and ordered the National Guard to join firefighting and law enforcement efforts. "This is an active and rapidly evolving situation and I urge everyone in the affected areas to remain vigilant and follow the direction of local officials," he said.The fire was caused by humans and first reported at 11:15 local time (18:15 GMT) on Saturday, according to local officials.The Washoe emergency information centre said around 15,000 acres (23 sq miles) had been burned. Chief Richard Edwards of the Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District - which covers the county said on Monday that the fire "continues to grow" and no  part of the fire's perimeter had yet been contained, CNN reported.Image source, Getty ImagesAround 13,700 homes were inside the evacuation area, local emergency services said, with two shelters set up to take in displaced residents.Of the six injured, three were emergency responders fighting the fire.Over the weekend, local officials described the fire as fast-moving, with windy weather and dry conditions contributing to its spread."The fire has definitely exploded in size," Lucia Starbuck, a local reporter for KUNR Public Radio, told the BBC. "It's burning these dry desert hills with neighbourhoods at the bottom. We know some homes have been burned, we don't know the exact number yet."Image source, Reuters/Nevada National GuardImage caption, The Nevada National Guard said 72 personnel, one Chinook and one Black Hawk helicopter had joined the responseAll Washoe County schools will be closed on Monday, except one, and mass road closures are in place. The immediate "go now" evacuation zone and wider "get set" area - where people are being warned to prepare to evacuate - do not extend to the centre of Reno, but do affect large urban areas and part of a highway.The University of Nevada in Reno - which has its main campus in the city, outside of but close to the "get set" warning area - said regular campus operations would continue but that it was monitoring the situation.Large air tankers and helicopters have been flying over the affected area dropping water and fire retardants.Image source, Justin DavisImage caption, Justin Davis, who lives close to Reno, said neighbour's properties were "completely levelled" by the fireJustin Davis, 29, lives on Peavine Mountain, close to Reno, and watched as the fire spread towards his home on Saturday and destroyed four of his vehicles.He told the BBC he had previously bought a water truck in case a wildfire like this occurred and had used it to save his home. "We turned on the water truck and just started spraying down the things we wanted to save," he said. The blaze has been been named the Hawk Fire because it was first reported near the Hawk Meadow Trail, to the west of Reno. Reno, in western Nevada, is located close to the state boundary with California and has a population of around 280,000 people.Wildfires are common in south-western US states, including Nevada, and are becoming more severe, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. There are currently three large fires in the state, out of a total of 79 nationwide.However, many of these fires develop in rural and less populated areas, with only a few encroaching on population centres.Scientists say that human-induced climate change makes the warm, dry conditions that facilitate the rapid spread of wildfires more likely.Are you in the area? If it is safe to do so, share your story.Get in touchAre you affected by the wildfires? If it is safe to do so, share your story.

schema.headline: Hawk fire: 90,000 told to evacuate as wildfire approaches Reno, Nevada

title: Graduate job vacancies drop by almost 50% in a year, survey suggests
description: The number of graduate jobs has fallen almost in half in the past year, according to new figures, as employers cut entry-level roles in favour of AI a
body: The number of graduate jobs has fallen almost in half in the past year, according to new figures, as employers cut entry-level roles in favour of AI and battle rising costs.Jobs website Adzuna said it had just 8,383 graduate vacancies listed in July, down from 15,397 at the same point last year.Adzuna also found competition among job seekers across all levels is rising, with an average of 2.14 job seekers per vacancy in July, up from 1.93 a year earlier.However, some have said the data might not be reflective of the whole graduate job market and may instead suggest a shift in the way the roles are advertised.Businesses have said employer national insurance and minimum wage hikes have made hiring more expensive, particularly for junior staff.The number of graduate vacancies listed hit its lowest level since Adzuna started recording such data in 2016. The firm pointed to a peak for graduate roles in 2017, when it had more than 55,800 listed on its website. That is more than six times the number of roles listed on the site in July. Andrew Hunter, the co-founder of Adzuna, said the figures show "employers still haven't found a reason to open up hiring" for recent graduates.But graduate jobs expert Charlie Ball said the numbers might not be as bad for graduates as they first appear.He said they could instead suggest that firms are advertising fewer roles specifically for graduates, even if the roles themselves still exist and end up being filled by graduates.From his experience in the sector, Ball said the graduate market has "not collapsed" but added: "We know the graduate jobs market is weak. We know it's not in great shape."Official figures show the UK's youth unemployment rate - which covers 16-to-24-year-olds - was 16.2% in the three months to March 2026. The number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) is now over one million.Young people have told BBC News previously they have applied for hundreds of jobs before even receiving a response.They also expressed frustration at the growing number of employers using AI to screen applications.Former government minister Alan Milburn is leading a major review of the youth unemployment crisis. He has previously said the number of entry-level jobs is shrinking, as is the number of part-time jobs traditionally filled by teenagers and students.The Adzuna data also showed vacancies for jobs in travel, teaching and construction rose in recent weeks.But sectors including healthcare, nursing, hospitality and logistics posted fewer vacancies.Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently changed the rules for public contracts so that companies bidding for them have to show how they will create jobs and training opportunities.A government spokesperson said on Monday: "The latest figures show there are 253,000 more people in work than this time last year with unemployment continuing to fall."We are determined to go further to restore opportunity for young people through our £2.5bn youth employment package which will deliver almost one million opportunities to earn or learn."

schema.headline: Graduate job vacancies drop by almost 50% in a year, survey suggests

title: Burnham to hand long-range missile blueprints as he visits Kyiv
description: Burnham vows support for Ukraine despite 'outrageous threats' from RussiaFigure caption, Is UK's Storm Shadow missile a game changer for Ukraine?ByHen
body: Burnham vows support for Ukraine despite 'outrageous threats' from RussiaFigure caption, Is UK's Storm Shadow missile a game changer for Ukraine?ByHenry Moore and Imogen JamesUpdated 2 hours agoAndy Burnham has promised to keep up the pressure on Russia despite Moscow's "outrageous threats", on his first official visit to Ukraine as UK prime minister.Burnham met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and chaired his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", set up by the UK and France under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.He said the coalition was "doing everything we can" while urging the US Congress to "ratchet up" economic pressure on Russia.The government has agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile - allowing Ukraine to produce the long-range weapon domestically.Burnham said allies were doing "everything we can" to "dig into our own stocks and help others dig into their stocks" of air defences to protect Ukraine."This is the moment to keep up the pressure on Russia, the moment to squeeze their ability to fund this illegal war," Burnham said, praising the "strength" of the Ukrainian people. "Ukraine has been Europe's protector, not a drain on our security but the front line in keeping Europe safe."It comes after Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov criticised the UK's decision to share the missile blueprints. Peskov said it prevented "even the slightest progress" towards achieving peace.He told reporters on Monday that the Russian military was already gathering data to locate any missile production sites to destroy them."Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime. Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire," he added.In response, Burnham said: "Who started the fire? That's the question, isn't it?"He said the issue of missile interceptors would be the main topic at the coalition of the willing meeting. Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Burnham accepts an award from Volodymyr Zelensky on behalf of the British people recognising the UK's support for UkraineImage source, ReutersImage caption, Burnham chaired his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing" in KyivBurnham has been reaffirming the UK's backing for Kyiv in the wake of escalating Russian strikes on Ukraine in recent weeks - including one on a shopping centre on Friday that killed at least 16 people. In a joint statement after the meeting, Burnham and co-chairs French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the group would aim to strength Kyiv's air defences "as a matter or urgent priority".They also condemned Moscow's "systemic and escalating strikes against Ukraine's cities, critical infrastructure and civilians" and pledged to "constrain Russia's war chest through sanctions and actions against the "shadow fleet".The Coalition of the Willing is a partnership of 34 countries including Ukraine. Members met on Monday in either Kyiv or by video conference, with a release stating "leaders once again reaffirmed their commitment to support Ukraine's independence".It came as the European Union said it had released €6.1bn (£5.2bn) in military aid for Ukraine to boost its air defences. The finance is part of a wider €90bn loan from the EU to Ukraine.The UK and Ukraine have also announced a new military technology partnership, external giving British experts access to Kyiv's Avengers AI Labs database. Downing Street says Ukraine has used sensors and cameras to capture data across the battlefield and it can be used to train AI models "to solve key national security challenges" faced by both countries.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Burnham lays flowers at the graves of Ukrainian soldiers during a Monday serviceOn Monday morning the prime minister laid flowers at the graves of Ukrainian soldiers during a service at the National Military Memorial Cemetery.He accepted an award from Zelensky on behalf of the British people recognising the UK's support for Ukraine during an independence day event outside the St Sofia cathedral in Kyiv. In a speech, Burnham compared Ukraine's resistance to Russia to the UK's fight with Nazi Germany, saying: "My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century, you hold that flame in the 21st."In a statement issued ahead of the visit, the prime minister said: "On Ukraine's 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes."I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine's security is our security."He said the friendship Ukraine shared with the UK would "long outlast Russia's illegal war", adding: "Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace."Moscow earlier warned of "consequences" over the use of British drones by Ukraine in its recent ramping up of strikes on Russian infrastructure.Kyiv has stepped up long-range attacks on Moscow and other Russian regions, targeting oil refineries and warehouses of the country's largest online retailer, Wildberries.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesThe government is allowing UK defence company MBDA to declassify information on its components for the Scalp missile, as Ukraine and France aim to establish assembly lines in Ukraine.Scalp missiles and its UK-produced version, the Storm Shadow, have already been provided to Kyiv by both Britain and France and used to hit military targets inside Russia.What are the Storm Shadow missiles Ukraine has fired into Russia?Ukraine hopes it can also be given more Patriot interceptor missiles, with Zelensky again asking for more of the weapon, which are used to combat Russia's ballistic missiles. Ukraine has been relying on American supplies of the Patriots, but its stockpiles are running low due to the war in Iran, leaving Ukraine vulnerable to Russian attacks.The Russian embassy in the UK has accused Britain of "deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis", saying "the deeper its involvement in the conflict... the higher the price it will pay".In response, Burnham said last week: "We are not fair-weather friends, we will be there in Ukraine's hour of need and that won't change."Asked on Tuesday about the Russian threat, Burnham maintained the UK was "providing support so that Ukraine can defend itself and that's been the British position all the way through this conflict, by previous prime ministers - it remains the case with me".The visit comes as Russia confirmed its ambassador to the UK, Andrei Kelin, had left his post in London in recent weeks.The Kremlin is yet to put forward a replacement but Russia's embassy to the UK told the BBC it did not reflect an intention to downgrade diplomatic relations between the two nations.Deadly exchanges between Russia and Ukraine continued overnight, with two children killed and seven injured when Ukrainian drone debris hit a private children's centre in Russia, local authorities say.A warehouse belonging to online retailer Ozon was also set on fire, two days after Ukraine said it would target the company for selling dual use items that could be used by the military.It was at the third night in the row that Ozon's warehouses had been targeted, with the company confirming on Saturday that a logistics centre in the Samara region had been hit and a warehouse in Orenburg on Sunday.Three people were also killed in a Russian attack on the north-eastern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv, regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

title: World's oceans hit highest temperature on record as El Niño grows
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByMark PoyntingClimate reporterUpdated 3 hours agoThe world's oceans are hotter than ever recorded, new data suggests, as th
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByMark PoyntingClimate reporterUpdated 3 hours agoThe world's oceans are hotter than ever recorded, new data suggests, as they suffer from human-caused climate change and the growing El Niño weather phenomenon.The average surface temperature of the planet's seas outside the polar regions hit 21.1C (70F) on Saturday, according to figures from the European Copernicus climate change service.That edges past the 21.09C recorded on three separate days in March 2024, and is far above average for the time of year.Warmer oceans can have wide-reaching consequences, including supercharging extreme weather, raising sea levels and harming marine life."This record is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress," said Dr Samantha Burgess, deputy director of Copernicus."El Niño is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming," she added.The data is based on sea temperatures 10m (32ft 10in) below the surface, using measurements from buoys, ships and satellites, which are combined to produce a global estimate.While the margin of record is currently very small and any global estimate comes with uncertainties, scientists say its timing is particularly notable. Average worldwide sea temperatures tend to reach their yearly peak in March or April, which corresponds to the end of summer in the southern hemisphere - and not in August.The southern hemisphere contains more of the planet's ocean surface than the northern hemisphere and so exerts a bigger influence on average sea temperatures.What is especially concerning to scientists is that the oceans are already so hot when the natural El Niño weather phenomenon is still some way off its expected peak.El Niño brings unusually warm waters to the surface of the eastern and central tropical Pacific Ocean. Warmer waters across such a large area means that global average temperatures typically spike too.El Niño is expected to keep strengthening until Christmas time, with scientists warning that it is on course to be the strongest in centuries.This could see ocean temperatures climb yet further."The fact that we are already breaking records is an early indicator of how strong the El Niño is becoming," said Dr Jeremy Grist, senior research fellow at the National Oceanography Centre in Southampton. "All things being equal we might expect the ocean temperature record to be broken again in March [or] April 2027," he added. The waters far away from El Niño's Pacific hunting ground are also extremely warm, including around the UK and Europe.The western English Channel has seen almost continuous marine heatwave conditions for more than three years, peaking at 7C above normal in July, according to Prof Tim Smyth, director of science at Plymouth Marine Laboratory.“This is unprecedented,” he added.Scientists say such widespread warmth around the planet is a clear sign of the growing effect that human-caused climate change is having on the world's seas. The oceans take up more than 90% of the excess heat trapped by humanity's greenhouse gas emissions, mainly from burning fossil fuels. "The latest Copernicus data reinforce the troubling upward trend in ocean temperatures,” said Smyth.Warmer seas help to fuel more extreme weather. They can provide storms with extra moisture and energy, and can intensify heatwaves on land in some coastal regions by reducing the cooling effect of sea breezes.Warmer water also takes up more space, raising sea levels and bringing a greater risk of coastal flooding - while intense ocean heat can be devastating for sea habitats, such as coral reefs.The increasing frequency of marine heatwaves is already "putting increasing pressure on marine ecosystems and the communities that depend on them", Burgess said.Figure caption, Watch: How does El Niño affect world weather?Get in touchWhat questions or concerns do you have about El Niño?

schema.headline: World's oceans hit highest temperature on record as El Niño grows

title: Toddler with sun allergy can now play in daylight thanks to UV film
description: Mollie's mother, Kirsty Campbell, 35, a charge nurse, said her daughter is at risk of sunburn all year round - and has previously burnt in November.Sh
body: Mollie's mother, Kirsty Campbell, 35, a charge nurse, said her daughter is at risk of sunburn all year round - and has previously burnt in November.She said: "The only time it's safe to go outside is in the dark. I want to keep her inside at all times to keep her safe, but we can't do that – she needs some sort of normality."The NHS had paid to install the film at Kirsty's home, but Mollie's parents live apart and there was no funding for it at her father Ryan's home, where she spends much of her time. The Archie Foundation, which provides support to babies, children and families during a hospital stay or after a bereavement, has now stepped in to cover the £600 cost."Their support has been indescribable – they've been a massive help for us," Kirsty said."I cried for about 20 minutes when I was told the money would come through. Mollie wouldn't have the same quality of life at her dad's house without it.She added: "It means she can do simple things like look outside for the postman or draw in daylight. "My ex-partner was having to take playpark equipment into his house as it wasn't safe outside. She's so happy running around like a normal child."

schema.headline: Toddler with sun allergy can now play in daylight thanks to UV film

title: Organised crime arrests as police investigate A66 crash that killed seven
description: Twelve people have been arrested as part of the investigation into the A66 crash that killed seven people, including two police officers.Nine men and
body: Twelve people have been arrested as part of the investigation into the A66 crash that killed seven people, including two police officers.Nine men and three women, aged between 19 and 61, have been arrested across Teesside on suspicion of a range of offences including possession of a firearm and being part of an organised crime group.In the early hours of Saturday, a Volkswagen Passat that had been pursued by police travelled the wrong way down the A66 near Middlesbrough and crashed into an oncoming police car - two PCs and all five Passat occupants died.Cleveland Police said it was investigating "serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident".PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and 17-year-old Cole Robert Worthy.Earlier, Cleveland Police released more details of its investigation into the lead-up to the crash and information about the 12 people it had arrested.The force said:It received several reports of two vehicles "being driven dangerously" on Saturday morningThe first vehicle, believed to be a Volvo XC60, was seen "ramming properties" in the Middlesbrough areaThe second vehicle, a Passat, is believed to have been associated with this activityBoth vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technologyThe Volvo has been recovered in MiddlesbroughFour of the five people in the Passat had previous convictionsAssistant Chief Constable Wayne Fox said the investigation had been "fast moving and complex".He said: "The events of that tragic night will have a lasting and profound impact on the Cleveland area and the communities we seek to protect."We have a duty to respond to, and thoroughly investigate, the serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident and to bring all those responsible to justice."An online fundraiser set up for the officers' families by the Cleveland Police Federation has raised more than £500,000.PC Blades' wife said he "gave his life in the line of duty, protecting and serving others with courage, dedication and selflessness".Before joining Cleveland Police, PC Blades worked as an English teacher at Carmel College in Darlington.The college said: "Many within our community will remember Matty as an intelligent, kind and approachable teacher, a valued colleague and someone who gave generously of himself to the young people in his care."The family of PC Clough described the former soldier as "our hero".They said he "jumped into action whenever needed" and was "willing to help anyone for any reason".The family statement added that he "proudly fought for his country to make the world a better place".Flags at Cleveland Police headquarters are flying at half-mast and Redcar and Cleveland Council has opened a book of condolence at its offices on Ridley Street in Redcar.Floral tributes can also be left at the memorial garden at the force's headquarters in Hemlington or any Cleveland Police station, the council said.Tributes for the five young men have also been shared on social media, with many of their friends saying they were "heartbroken" and "lost for words". Balloon releases have been announced in their memory.Follow BBC Tees on X,, external Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Tees on BBC Sounds.

schema.headline: Organised crime arrests as police investigate A66 crash that killed seven

title: Divorce, smartphones and control - BBC sees how Taliban run Afghanistan
description: Figure caption, Watch: Eighteen-year-old woman argues her case for a divorce, saying her "honour and dignity have already been ruined"ByKawoon Khamoos
body: Figure caption, Watch: Eighteen-year-old woman argues her case for a divorce, saying her "honour and dignity have already been ruined"ByKawoon KhamooshBBC World ServiceReporting fromSheberghan, Kabul and KandaharGovernor Abdullah Sarhadi gives money to treat a boy's broken arm and hands out funds for a local mosque - then, in his office in northern Afghanistan, an astonishing exchange unfolds.A young woman tells the grey-bearded former Taliban commander that she wants to divorce her husband, who she accuses of months of abuse and beatings.She will not take no for an answer.In a country where girls are banned from secondary education, the 18-year-old argues her case calmly and confidently, her face completely hidden behind a full-face veil and sunglasses."If there was any chance to live together, I wouldn't be here… I have taken my decision," she says.After trying to persuade her to avoid divorce, the governor later comments that women are "mindless" and "deficient in intellect", to laughter from the male officials, bodyguards and elders around him.The moment gives a rare glimpse into the day-to-day realities of the Taliban's rule, five years after they swept aside the US-backed government in 2021.Image caption, The governor of Jawzjan province, Abdullah Sarhadi, who fought for the Taliban was held in US detention in Guantanamo Bay for several years In that time, women have been excluded from most workplaces, banned from universities and may not travel alone or visit parks and leisure centres.In encounters spread over two years, the BBC gained unusual access to influential figures in the extreme Islamist movement, spending time with men who once planned suicide attacks or spent years in underground hideouts, but are now officials and soldiers.The Taliban came into power saying they had changed, but many of their policies are similar to the hard-line interpretation of Sharia - Islamic religious law - they imposed in the 1990s.The men we met seemed to want to present themselves as reasonable, yet were not keen to discuss their past violence. And we saw moments of unease between the rulers and those they rule.Governor Sarhadi says Tuba – not her real name – should stay in the marriage."Ask yourself: 'Who would marry me after I get my divorce?'" says Sarhadi. "You'll have to compromise a lot or you'll lose your dignity and honour.""Mr Governor, my honour and dignity have already been ruined," she responds.Her husband listens, awaiting his turn to speak.Under Sharia, a woman requesting that her husband agrees to a divorce may have to return some or all of the money given to her by him when they married. A financial settlement is often agreed. But this woman's husband says he wants four times the amount, which her family refuses to pay.The governor says the woman should be given her own room. He adds that officials will warn him not to beat her - "otherwise he'd be jailed".Unsatisfied, Tuba's father later tells the BBC the family will pursue divorce through the courts, even though, under the Taliban's court system, it is very difficult for a woman to get a divorce without the husband's consent.Image source, EPA/REX/ShutterstockImage caption, A hole left by the destruction of one of the Buddha statues in Bamiyan -  Sarhadi says he destroyed itSarhadi was a military commander during the Taliban's first stint in power in the 1990s. He was among thousands of insurgents who surrendered in late 2001 as a US-led coalition ousted the group.He was held for several years in US detention in Guantanamo Bay, but eventually released.When the Taliban regained power, he became a governor - first in the province of Bamiyan, then when we met him in late June, in Sheberghan city in Jawzjan province. He has recently become deputy commander of a military corps in the northern province of Kunduz.Tapping on an old-style mobile with a tiny screen, he says a recent ban on smartphones for officials has slowed things down. "Before, you could send a quick message… sending documents and getting an answer fast." If he says any more about the ban, "it will cause trouble", he adds.But in other ways his worldview seems largely unchanged from the Taliban's position 25 years ago. Then, he was a military commander in Bamiyan, where the Taliban blew up ancient giant Buddha statues, triggering international shock and condemnation.He initially tries to avoid our questions about the archaeological site, but eventually, he says: "I destroyed it with my own hands."Whatever we did and we do is in accordance with the guidance and God's law… We smash idols rather than sell them. Why should I regret? It was God's will."In the capital Kabul, we meet another senior Taliban figure who swapped a violent past for a role with the ruling administration.Habibullah Badr drives us through the streets in an armoured car.He says he was previously "responsible for the operations of suicide attackers" in Kabul."I know all the roads and streets very well… we had all the information we needed about Kabul and its alleys," he says. "There were areas that needed a long time to plan."Taliban suicide attacks killed thousands of people in Afghanistan, including many civilians.Badr is cautious about discussing his past though, fearing it will "make people upset" and could "reopen wounds".Asked about civilian deaths, he says the Taliban targeted US convoys and that civilians were urged to stay away from foreign bases.Whenever I try to ask him about specific attacks that took place in civilian areas, he evades the question.Image caption, Habibullah Badr says that in the past he was involved in operations involving suicide attacksHe is currently taking time out from official roles for medical treatment, but was previously deputy head of prisons for the whole country – and ran the very jail where he was held on death row under the previous government.Badr invites us to join him at a tribal gathering, where the head of a charitable foundation is to honour him with a medal. But things take an unexpected turn."Mr Badr is a pride for Afghanistan and a great fighter," says Sultan Mohammad Talaee. "But I also have a complaint. If the schools and education were open to all it would be a great work for Afghanistan. I hope this doesn't offend you."An awkward silence follows, his audience unsure how to react. Talaee's microphone is swiftly removed.Afterwards, he tells the BBC: "I requested for the girls' schools to reopen… seeking knowledge is an obligation for both men and women in Islam."He adds: "There were other things I wanted to say but they didn't let me talk more."The Taliban: Coming Out of the ShadowsAudiences in the UK can watch on iPlayer from 17:00 and on Global Eye on BBC Two at 19:00Often those who speak out face much more severe consequences.Women told us of the deep despair they felt over dreams thwarted by restrictions on education, and of friends jailed for protesting.Most journalists we spoke to said they had been summoned or questioned by the Taliban's intelligence organisation, Estikhbaraat.The BBC put some of these concerns to the Taliban government's spokesman, known as Zabihullah Mujahid.Image caption, Zabihullah Mujahid says women's rights and freedom of speech need to be seen "through the Sharia lens"He has been a public face for the Taliban government since 2021. He still uses the pseudonym he went by for years during the insurgency, but he told us his real name is Tahir Shah Seddiqi - revealing it publicly for the first time.In a lavish press centre funded by the Americans for the previous government, we ask him about the first press conference he gave there, two days after the Taliban took control of the country.Then, he told the world the Taliban government would allow women to work and study "within our frameworks" and they would "be very active" in society. Why did they fail to keep their word?"We are committed to women's rights, freedom of speech and other things within Sharia," he replies. "We should see everything through the Sharia lens."Allowing women to work in offices such as his own "would lead to immoralities" and "their dignity would be undermined", he adds.He says the issue of education for women is "under discussions… we need a Sharia-based solution for it".When questioned about the Taliban's crackdown on media freedom, he says: "In a society like Afghanistan we have our restrictions. We can't let media do whatever propaganda they want… they can't broadcast against Islamic laws and rites."The Taliban government sits in Kabul, but Mujahid spends a lot of time in the southern city of Kandahar, the Taliban's heartland, which some now consider the de facto capital.We ask to meet the Taliban's supreme leader, Hibatullah Akhundzada, who is based there. He rarely appears in public and has never given a media interview - we are told it will not be possible at the moment.Restrictions have been tightened in Kandahar since I last visited two years ago. Now men must have beards. Radio stations are not allowed to play music or broadcast women's voices, and we were not allowed to film in the city.Two hours' drive away, along dusty roads, some of the group's most devoted former fighters showed the BBC the insurgents' old secret cave network.Abid Lalai, a former fighter who now mans a checkpoint as part of a security force under the interior ministry, shows us the holes he fired from and the places he used to put his Quran and hang AK-47s.Image caption, Abid Lalai is one of many Taliban fighters who hid out in caves to evade capture under previous governmentsHis superior, Abdul Samad, shows us an unmarked graveyard, saying his father is buried here, killed fighting for the Taliban.The area is one of the most deprived in a country where the UN says three in four people cannot provide for their basic needs. Samad says the local population desperately need water, roads and clinics."Emirate [Taliban] officials have not forgotten us," says Samad. He says the leaders may be busy with other priorities. "We are hopeful, they will look after us sometime."Five years since the Taliban began their second stint in power, poverty, unemployment and economic instability remain pressing concerns.Taliban figures we spoke to said they were working to tackle them, but we met other people who believe the group itself is the country's main problem."I'm speechless about how a group that has no understanding about life is suddenly in power," says Hoda - not her real name - a woman who protested on the streets when the Taliban first returned to power."Women can't accept this situation," she tells the BBC. "They might advance restrictions but it won't stay like this forever.""I think the Taliban are scared of educated women," she adds. "That's why they restrict women. They want uneducated women so they can't raise wise men. Because that would end the Taliban."Additional reporting by Hafizullah Maroof

schema.headline: Divorce, smartphones and control - BBC sees how Taliban run Afghanistan

title: Iran faces 'greatest financial offensive ever', says US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent
description: The US announced a host of sanctions against Iran and threatened its supporters in what Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said was "the single greatest
body: The US announced a host of sanctions against Iran and threatened its supporters in what Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said was "the single greatest financial offensive ever".Labelling it an "economic D-Day" for Iran, Bessent said the US would sever all economic ties with the country and added that any nation financially partnering with Iran would also be isolated. However, the latest threat to the Iranian regime follows several U-turns and extended deadlines from the White House in its efforts to end the conflict.The war has led to hikes in global oil prices, and in response to the latest threat Iran warned it would shut down all oil exports from the region if the war continued.The Iranian regime has also issued a fresh warning to shipping to not pass through the Strait of Hormuz without its permission, according to Reuters.One fifth of the world's oil and gas usually passes through strait, a narrow waterway south of Iran, but the flow has been effectively blocked by the country since the conflict began at the end of February, leading to higher oil prices globally.At a press conference on Monday outlining what has been called "Operation Economic Outcast", Bessent said the US was launching an "economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe"."Iran now faces a very clear choice with only two paths before them: complete global isolation....or a path back to normalcy with an opportunity to rejoin the global economy," he said.The treasury secretary claimed America was "no longer managing the Iranian threat, we are ending it".Bessent said the Treasury Department had mapped networks, facilitators and financial channels used by Iran to evade sanctions to trade oil.The department said it has issued determinations against five sectors: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. The Treasury has also imposed sanctions on almost 60 entities, individuals and vessels.Bessent said that such actions would "tighten the noose and block every potential source of revenue" for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the wider Iranian regime. In a warning to governments and entities assisting or trading with Iran, he said they could not "claim they are blind to enabling this activity".He declined to highlight specific countries, but said Trump would be phoning world leaders "with specific request to cease their interactions with the regime."While he said it was important to give people time to understand the new sanctions, he added: "they should know that that will move very quickly and that we are serious."David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, cast doubt on the effectiveness of the sanctions announcement."With the renewed US naval blockade already strangling Iran's oil exports, the direct impact of 'economic D-Day' on Iran's energy revenues will be somewhat of a damp squib," he said."We suspect that the new package will have only a limited direct impact on Iranian energy flows in the short term."He said that was partly due to the fact roughly 90% of Iran's oil goes to China, a country "which has not recognised US sanctions in the past and is unlikely to be cowed this time either".Over the course of the conflict so far, previous threats have included Trump saying in April that "a whole civilisation will die tonight" unless Iran agreed a deal to end the war and unblock the Strait of Hormuz.The US eventually climbed down from that position after mediator Pakistan intervened and called for more diplomacy.The economic impact of the Iran war is being felt in the US and across the world. Higher oil prices have fuelled concerns over the cost of living, with petrol and diesel  prices much higher than they were a year ago. In the US, gasoline prices have surpassed $4 a gallon and affordability is among the top concerns of American voters ahead of the mid-term elections in November.On Monday, a barrel of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil prices, was $92.Last week, Bessent announced the US government would intervene in the bond markets and buy back more government debt in a bid to boost demand for bonds and lower borrowing rates.But the impact of the announcenment was short-lived, with long-term borrowing costs bouncing back up a day later.

schema.headline: Iran faces 'greatest financial offensive ever', says US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent

title: Snooker champion Graeme Dott guilty of child sex abuse
description: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Graeme Dott was found guilty of two charges at the High Court in GlasgowByJames DelaneyBBC ScotlandUpdated 2 hour
body: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Graeme Dott was found guilty of two charges at the High Court in GlasgowByJames DelaneyBBC ScotlandUpdated 2 hours agoFormer world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been found guilty of child sexual abuse.The 49-year-old denied two charges of lewd and libidinous behaviour towards a girl and a boy between 1993 and 2010.During a trial, the High Court in Glasgow heard that Dott had exposed himself and inappropriately touched a primary school girl in the 1990s and attacked a young boy between 2006 and 2010.Lord Harrower told Dott, who won the World Snooker Championship in 2006, he would be sentenced at a separate hearing in Edinburgh on 29 September.Dott covered his face with his hands and shook his head while the verdict was delivered by jurors following a five-day trial.He previously called the allegations made against him "disgusting".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Dott won the world championship title in 2006Lewd and libidinous practices refer to any sexual crimes against children committed prior to 1 December 2010.The offence was abolished in 2009, but is still used for crimes carried out before then.During the trial, the court heard how Dott had "caressed" the girl's bottom while giving her a piggyback and that, on another occasion, he had exposed himself to her.On another occasion, she said Dott suggested she "take her trousers down" and lifted her top and began kissing her stomach after asking if she wanted to "play a guessing game".The girl, now a woman in her 40s, said Dott would kiss her, touch her inappropriately and carried out a sexual act that would, if committed now, amount to rape.She said she recalled the "smell" of creams Dott used for a skin condition after he kissed her and that the actions left her "shocked and scared".'Rewarded' with giftsThe court heard how Dott bought her a teddy bear with a love heart on it in the course of the abuse.Police previously contacted Dott about the allegations in 2001, but no charges were brought.The woman gave a new statement to police in 2025.During his evidence, the boy said his abuse at the hands of Dott began not long after he defeated Peter Ebdon to win his sole world title at The Crucible in Sheffield in 2006.The boy, now a man in his 20s, said he was about eight years old when Dott molested him in a shower at a home in South Lanarkshire.He told the court how Dott "rewarded" him with crisps and fizzy drinks and once handed him a £50 note, only to accuse the boy of stealing it when his parents found out he had the money.He also said he was abused in a car on a number of occasions and "inappropriately touched" while Dott played online poker.Figure caption, Snooker champion Graeme Dott guilty of child sex abuseDott had told the trial the allegations were false and that he had "never acted inappropriately with anyone".Det Insp Gary Smillie, of Police Scotland, described Dott as a "dangerous individual".He added: "I hope this conviction provides some measure of comfort to those impacted by his crimes."His conviction is as a direct result of their strength in coming forward and providing information which assisted our inquiries."Lord Harrower was told the woman had provided a victim impact statement for him to consider before sentencing next month.Dott was taken into custody until then.Removed from sport The World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association (WPBSA) said it had permanently revoked Dott's membership with immediate effect.This followed an emergency board meeting board where it was unanimously agreed to removed him from the sport.The WPBSA has also written to World Snooker Tour (WST) to request his immediate removal from the WST Hall of Fame.Dott was previously suspended from all professional snooker activities on 9 April 2025 pending the outcome of his trial.He was subsequently relegated from the professional ranking list at the conclusion of the 2025/26 season.

schema.headline: Snooker champion Graeme Dott guilty of child sex abuse

title: Prince Harry steps down from African Parks charity board
description: The Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of an African wildlife charity whose rangers had been found to have committed human rights abuses a
body: The Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of an African wildlife charity whose rangers had been found to have committed human rights abuses against indigenous people.A spokesman for Prince Harry confirmed he was stepping down after being president for the charity, African Parks, for six years before becoming a member of its board of directors in 2023, but said he remains a "supporter of its mission".Last year the organisation admitted human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in Congo-Brazzaville.Prince Harry's resignation comes shortly after it was announced he was relocating with the Duchess of Sussex, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet from California to the UK.Prince Harry's spokesman said "the Duke is proud of his 10 years with African Parks and fully supports the ongoing strengthening of its board."His commitment to conservation in Africa continues, and he remains a supporter of African Parks' mission."African Parks manages around 20 national parks and protected areas across 12 countries.It was subject to an independent human rights investigation into allegations guards managed and paid by the charity had beaten, raped and tortured indigenous people in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park.The charity said in 2025 it had improved its safeguarding processes both in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park and institutionally. Announcing a "governance refresh of its board of directors", the charity thanked Prince Harry for his association, saying he had "brought global attention to the urgent need for biodiversity protection for the benefit of people and wildlife, and has contributed greatly to promoting philanthropy for the cause of conservation in Africa".It added: "The duke remains deeply committed to this cause, and remains a strong supporter of African Parks' work."The charity's website says Prince Harry served as part of the expert team that helped implement the first phase of the 500 Elephants project, which was "one of the largest and most significant elephant translocations in conservation history".It saw wildlife experts move elephants from a park in Malawi to help increase population in areas where they have been heavily poached.Prince Harry has said helping move elephants to safer homes was an "amazing" experience.The Sussexes are back in the spotlight after the revelation last week they were returning to the UK this month after enrolling their children to start at a British school in September.No change is expected to the official status of Prince Harry and Meghan and they will remain as private individuals.Their pending return to the UK has raised questions on their security arrangements.Last year, Prince Harry lost a legal challenge over the levels of security he and his family are entitled to while in the UK.It is unclear what provisions will be made for their security once they return to the UK.The couple's plans while they are in the UK are also unclear. The BBC learned the Duchess of Sussex was in talks to return to acting with a role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, which would be her first significant acting role since her marriage to Prince Harry.In early 2020, the Sussexes left the UK and stepped back from their royal duties before settling in California in March that year.

schema.headline: Prince Harry steps down from African Parks charity board
